channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated papers, news and policy on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: DelusionEval: Measuring Delusion-Linked Behaviors in AI Chatbots
item.description: An evaluation protocol built from real episodes of psychological harm rather than synthetic vignettes, prompting each model with 589 conversation histories drawn from 18 people who experienced delusions, comprising 12,591 messages. Delusion linked behavior does not track model size, release date or the presence of test time reasoning, so newer and larger is not safer, and every model family tested showed substantial rates. The sharpest finding concerns context length, since prepending 350 additional messages raised the rate of failing to discourage self harm from 30.0 to 41.1 percent, which means short prompt benchmarks systematically understate the risk that accumulates over a long relationship with a chatbot.

item.title: Psychosis Risk and Generative Artificial Intelligence Use Frequency, Motivations, and Delusion-Like Experiences
item.description: A cross sectional survey of 1,003 young adults in the United States compared people at elevated psychosis risk with their peers and found the difference is not whether they use generative AI but how. Elevated risk respondents were no more likely to have ever used a chatbot, yet were considerably more likely to use it intensively, meaning several times a day, more than thirty minutes a day, or six or more conversations a day, with odds ratios from 1.70 to 2.56. They more often sought social and emotional support and ascribed human roles such as companion, friend, therapist and romantic partner, with odds ratios reaching 3.08, and delusion related interactions were endorsed by 13.3 to 30.7 percent of the at risk group. Intensity and relational framing, not adoption, are the clinically useful signals.

item.title: Mass Media Narratives of Psychiatric Adverse Events Associated With Generative AI Chatbots
item.description: A rapid scoping review mapping how press coverage constructs the evidence base that regulators and clinicians actually encounter, since almost everything known publicly about chatbot linked psychiatric harm arrives first as journalism. Reporting concentrates on the most severe outcomes, especially youth suicide deaths, and is usually framed around regulatory and corporate accountability rather than clinical mechanism, which skews what gets counted as a harm at all. The authors are careful that causality cannot be established from media reports, but the recurring pattern of high intensity interaction, pre existing user vulnerability and thin safeguard disclosure is itself the argument for structured safety surveillance and transparent risk auditing.

item.title: A systematic review of machine learning techniques to address diagnosis and treatment of autism
item.description: A review of 55 studies published between 2017 and 2023 on machine learning applied to autism diagnosis and treatment, cataloguing which techniques, features and datasets recur and where the field has concentrated its attention. Because the causes of autism remain unsettled, the work leans on feature identification and hidden correlations as the route to earlier diagnosis, which is precisely where the ethical stakes sit, since a model that predicts a label without a mechanism can still change how a child is treated. The most useful part for a responsible AI reader is the map of which datasets the field keeps reusing, because a reused dataset propagates whatever narrowness it was built with.

item.title: Reasonable adjustments for neurodivergent students in higher education: generative AI, accessibility, and mediated authorship
item.description: An argument that large language models belong in the same category as note takers, scribes and readers rather than in the category of academic misconduct, since higher education has long accepted mediated authorship as a legitimate accommodation. The test proposed is provenance of ideas rather than provenance of sentences, so what matters is whether the intellectual work originates with the student, and on that test tools used to summarise reading, structure an assignment or unblock a draft count as adjustments rather than shortcuts. The counterweight the paper takes seriously is that these systems encode pedagogical models built on neurotypical assumptions and can quietly invalidate nonlinear ways of learning even while removing a barrier.

item.title: Teens Are Turning to Chatbots for Mental Health Help. We Need Rules to Keep Them Safe
item.description: A commentary drawing the policy lesson from the JAMA Pediatrics finding that youth use of chatbots for mental health advice rose from roughly one in eight to one in five in a single year, an increase of more than forty percent. The argument is explicitly comparative, since with social media adoption outran the debate about causation and Congress never passed meaningful national protections for children, and the claim here is that the chatbot timeline is still early enough to build something sturdier. What that requires is rules written before the evidence is complete rather than after it is too late, which is the opposite of how the last platform cycle went.

item.title: Health advisory: Use of generative AI chatbots and wellness applications for mental health
item.description: A formal advisory that places the surge in chatbot use in its structural context, meaning unmet demand for care, too few providers in rural and under resourced communities, and a payment system that discourages clinicians from accepting insurance, so people substitute what is available for what is needed. The APA does not recommend general purpose generative AI chatbots for psychological treatment, noting that these products are mostly not designed to give clinical feedback, often lack scientific validation and oversight, and frequently ship without adequate safety protocols. The accompanying 2026 survey shows this is not hypothetical, since 77 percent of psychologists report patients telling them they use AI and more than a third say patients treat it as an additional provider.
